posts.title: We Warned the World About AI in 2015. How Did We Do?
posts.description: In 2015, I signed an open letter alongside Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak, Jensen Huang, and some of the most accomplished minds in artificial intelligence, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Demis Hassabis. Among the other signatories were Ilya Sutskever and Dario Amodei, who would go on to help build some of the very technologies about which we were expressing concern. Eleven years later, I’m a founder of Sphere , one of the fastest-growing AI companies in the world. Some of the questions we raised in that letter are now questions I have to answer in the course of running a business. The letter, organized by the Future of Life Institute, was titled Research Priorities for Robust and Beneficial Artificial Intelligence . It is worth reading again. What strikes me most about it today is how optimistic it was. We contemplated the possibility of eradicating disease and poverty. posts.title: How Disney Turned the Future Into a Theme Park
posts.description: I recently learned about the history of EPCOT, and it made me sick to my stomach. No, it MAKES me sick to my stomach, and I can’t stop thinking about it. Not because I dislike Disney World. Quite the opposite. I have enormous admiration for Walt Disney, for what he created, and for the extraordinary imagination required to build things the world had never seen before. But here’s the thing: EPCOT was never supposed to be a theme park. It was supposed to be Walt Disney’s greatest contribution to humanity. Instead, the people entrusted with his company, his resources, and his legacy built another tourist attraction. The Dream Was Never About Another Theme Park By the mid-1960s, Walt Disney had already accomplished more than most people could imagine in a dozen lifetimes. posts.title: Two Wings
posts.description: My 16-year-old daughter got a tattoo. I know how I am supposed to respond: anger, disappointment, frustration, but I am not any of those things. I am proud of her. I have hesitated to write about this because grief is not content. These children were not characters in a news story. They were real people. They were my daughter’s friends. They had parents who loved them, futures waiting for them, and ordinary plans for a morning they never got to see. On January 29, 2025, a plane carrying young skaters, their families, and their coaches home from the National Development Training Camp collided with a military helicopter near Washington, D.C. Of the sixty-seven people who perished on that flight, twenty-eight members of the figure skating community. The young skaters who died were kids my daughter had grown up with, kids she had skated with. They were her friends, and two of them … two of them were her best friends. She was 14 years old.
